problem: Applying reinforcement learning to real robots needs a state representation extracted from complex raw sensor data (video). Prior approaches rely on hand-crafted heuristics, and raw images are unsuitable for linear value approximators such as LSPI.
motivation: Biology (rodent place cells learned by slow feature analysis, Franzius et al.) suggests an unsupervised way to learn state filters automatically. SFA on a random walk converges to trigonometric polynomials of the robot state, which are known to approximate continuous functions well under linear models. This makes SFA a natural preprocessing for LSPI.
key_idea: Learn kernel SFA filters from a random-walk video of a head-mounted camera and feed their outputs as state features to LSPI to learn a discrete-action navigation control from single images.
insight: Trigonometric-like SFA features support linear Q-value approximation: with ideal trigonometric responses about 20-40 filters give near-reference policies, while too many filters cause overfitting and unstable policy iteration. With real (simulated) video far more filters are needed (80-500 in the working regime, about 2-3 extra steps) because SFA output deviates from ideal responses and noise causes erratic behaviour where Q-values are close. Slowness converges toward the optimum as the number of support vectors grows, and higher image resolution is worse at equal model complexity.
method: Random-walk data: record one random-walk video (35128 frames at ~1 Hz) with a head-mounted camera, giving training sets for both SFA and LSPI; images are clipped, brightness-corrected and shrunk to 32x16 RGB.

Kernel SFA: centering, sphering and slowness minimization performed on an RBF kernel matrix with projected-process approximation over greedily selected support vectors (nu=0.1, sigma varied), complexity O(m^2 n).

LSPI (LSQ/LSTD): linear Q-value estimation on SFA outputs for 3 discrete actions (forward ~30cm, turn left/right ~45 deg), gamma=0.9 (0.95 in two-room), reward +1 in the goal area and -1 near walls (<50cm).
Modified initial policy: use all actions at once, equivalent to a random policy, to reduce initial-policy dependence and double the working regime.
Convergence quality C(pi): mean ratio V^pi/V^pi* (gamma^(steps-1)) compared to a hand-crafted greedy reference policy using true coordinates.
Control: at each step compute the SFA filters on the current image and take the action with the highest Q-value.

setting.backbone: Kernel SFA (RBF, support vectors up to <8000) + LSPI linear Q-function, trained from scratch
setting.training_data: Single random-walk video in the target room: 35128 frames (robot); LSPI set of 11656 transitions (robot), 50,000 transitions (two-room sim)
setting.observation: monocular RGB from a head-mounted camera (left Bumblebee image, 66 deg FOV), downscaled to 32x16
setting.action_space: 3 discrete actions: move forward ~30 cm, turn left/right ~45 deg
setting.simulator: Custom Java3D simulator plus real Pioneer 3DX robot in a 3m x 1.8m arena
setting.privileged: Ceiling-camera positions used for reward computation and evaluation during training/testing; ultrasonic sensors used only to avoid walls during random-walk recording; no privileged info at policy execution

numbers.eval_set_note: 20 test trajectories with real Pioneer robot, from arbitrary start positions
numbers.extra: Two goal areas tested; success rate reported in abstract as approximate
numbers.evidence: Abstract: 'allow the learned control to navigate successfully in ca. 80% of the test trials'

numbers_note: Only the approximate 80% real-robot success rate is stated; other results (convergence quality, extra steps) are in figures and described qualitatively (2-3 extra steps vs reference in simulation).
results: In the simulated rectangular room, SFA+LSPI with 80-500 filters reaches the working regime, differing by only about 2-3 steps per trajectory from a hand-crafted reference policy. On the real Pioneer robot with 128 filters, the goal was reached in about 80% of 20 test trajectories, though trajectories were surprisingly long and erratic. The two-room environment did not yield a working control, and no comparison against alternative representations such as SLAM was made.
limitations: Requires static, bounded, asymmetric environments and artificial illumination; SFA filters mix, so unwanted state components (humans, sun) cannot be excluded
Computationally heavy (O(d^3 a^3) LSPI, O(m^2 n) kernel SFA), only discrete actions, low resolution; two-room environment failed
Small real-robot evaluation (20 trials, ~80% success), erratic behaviour where Q-values are close, and no baseline comparisons (e.g. SLAM); many hyperparameters sensitive
builds_on: Franzius et al. place cells via SFA
compares_to: Hand-crafted reference policy (greedy using true coordinates)
